terms.label: AI-native
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary uses AI-native in a broad architectural sense and does not certify one universal definition. The label does not establish model quality, autonomy, safety, or correctness.
terms.short_definition: AI-native describes a system designed from the outset for AI to take part in its normal operation.
terms.reader_preview: AI-native describes a system designed from the outset for AI to take part in its normal operation.
terms.card_definition: In Plectis, agents read structured context, use tools, make bounded changes, and leave records that later work can inspect. The files, interfaces, and checks are arranged to support that participation.
terms.reader_rule: The term describes a design choice, not a measured level of intelligence or reliability.
terms.deep_definition: Human direction, permissions, and independent checks still matter. A workflow can be built around AI and still need substantial supervision or correction.
terms.scope_note: The term covers workflow architecture built around agent execution. It does not establish model quality, autonomy, safety, or correctness.
terms.example: A workflow in which an agent reads a source route, claims a file, performs a bounded change, runs a validator, and leaves a result record is AI-native.
terms.non_example: Adding a chat box to an otherwise unchanged application does not by itself make the application AI-native.

terms.label: algebraic number
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A complex number satisfying some nonzero polynomial equation with integer coefficients.
terms.reader_preview: A complex number satisfying some nonzero polynomial equation with integer coefficients.
terms.card_definition: Every rational number is algebraic because p/q solves qx-p=0. The irrational number √2 is algebraic because it solves x²-2=0.
terms.reader_rule: Algebraic does not mean rational. Numbers that satisfy no such integer polynomial, such as π, are called transcendental.
terms.deep_definition: The totient discussion explains that a digit-complexity theorem applying to algebraic irrationals cannot be used until algebraicity of the target sum is independently known.

terms.label: annex
terms.meaning_boundary: Here annex means curated external prior art adapted into the local doctrine graph, not merely an appendix attached to a document.

terms.reader_preview: An annex is Plectis's source-linked account of ideas or techniques drawn from an outside project.

terms.reader_rule: The original source remains the authority on what the outside project actually does.
terms.deep_definition: Adapting a technique requires a separate local decision and check; an annex does not establish that the technique has already been integrated or works here.

terms.label: anti-principle
terms.meaning_boundary: An anti-principle is a named shortcut this system refuses. It is not a moral prohibition, a legal ban, or a claim that the named pattern is always wrong outside this lattice.
terms.short_definition: An anti-principle names a recurring shortcut or failure pattern that the system is meant to avoid.
terms.reader_preview: An anti-principle names a recurring shortcut or failure pattern that the system is meant to avoid.
terms.card_definition: Where a principle describes a desired way of working, an anti-principle makes a specific bad practice recognisable. It connects the refusal to the requirement it protects, so the rule can be applied to real cases.
terms.reader_rule: The useful question is which concrete behaviour would violate the rule.
terms.deep_definition: For example, treating a plausible summary as evidence of a completed action would defeat a requirement to check the actual execution record.
terms.scope_note: Anti-principles appear as their own kind on the doctrine page and as numbered AP cards in the doctrine reference.

terms.label: Apache-2.0
terms.meaning_boundary: This registry only explains how the external term appears here. The external owner, specification, or primary source controls when exact meaning matters.

terms.reader_preview: Apache-2.0 is an open-source licence allowing use, modification, and redistribution, including commercial use, subject to its conditions.

terms.label: appeal lifecycle
terms.meaning_boundary: An appeal lifecycle is the system’s internal path for contesting and repairing a recorded judgment; it is not a legal appeal process or an informal objection left in chat.
terms.short_definition: An appeal lifecycle is the process for challenging a system decision and recording how the challenge was resolved.
terms.reader_preview: An appeal lifecycle is the process for challenging a system decision and recording how the challenge was resolved.
terms.card_definition: A disputed label or result is examined, its cause is identified, and responsibility for any repair is assigned. The outcome records the reasoning and supporting evidence so later work can tell whether the decision still stands.
terms.reader_rule: An appeal can confirm a decision, correct it, or reopen the question.
terms.deep_definition: Plectis uses the record to distinguish a faulty implementation from a faulty expectation: sometimes the check needs repair, and sometimes the rule being checked needs revision.
terms.scope_note: The term covers governance over contested judgments across the system, including challenges raised by operator review, route judgment, and projection checks. A reader meets it wherever a label or decision can be formally disputed and tracked to resolution.
terms.example: The operator-court appeal ledger is a concrete appeal lifecycle in use: entries record judgments that operators have challenged, the classified cause, and the rationale that closes each one, fed by the Cognitive Operator Registry that holds the operator contract.

example_route.label: Cognitive Operator Registry
example_route.gloss: open the component that records and validates operator-raised challenges

terms.non_example: An appeal lifecycle is not a legal court process and not a record of a row that errored and was discarded. It is the tracked path a deliberately contested judgment follows from challenge to recorded resolution.

terms.label: apply
terms.meaning_boundary: Apply names the governed mutation lane when used as an ai_workflow noun; it does not redefine the ordinary verb 'apply'.

terms.reader_preview: In Plectis, apply is the step that makes a specified change to a file or record.
terms.card_definition: It follows observation or a proposal by naming the target and performing the permitted operation. The operation should check the conditions for the change and validate the resulting state.
terms.reader_rule: A proposed change has not taken effect until the apply step succeeds.
terms.deep_definition: Recording the operation, target, and result makes later inspection possible. Where an operation is reversible, its record can also explain how to undo it without disturbing unrelated work.
terms.scope_note: The term covers the mutation lane of the system, the part that writes changes rather than merely reading or proposing them. A reader meets it on the architecture map, in the component that authorises governed mutation, and in the doctrine cards that mark what an unsafe apply looks like.

terms.label: arithmetic progression
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A sequence obtained by repeatedly adding one fixed difference.
terms.reader_preview: A sequence obtained by repeatedly adding one fixed difference.
terms.card_definition: The numbers 2,7,12,17,… form an arithmetic progression with first term 2 and common difference 5; its nth term is 2+5n under zero-based indexing.

terms.label: artifact
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: An artifact is a stored item that someone can inspect or use, such as a file, report, dataset, or generated page.
terms.reader_preview: An artifact is a stored item that someone can inspect or use, such as a file, report, dataset, or generated page.
terms.card_definition: Plectis uses the term for the concrete objects its work produces and maintains. An artifact has an identity and a role; it may be original source material, a record of an action, or a view generated from other data.

terms.label: audit

terms.short_definition: An audit is a systematic examination of records against stated requirements; here it often checks whether an agent's report matches its actions.

terms.card_definition: For example, a completion audit can compare a claim that tests passed with the commands and results recorded for that session. This is narrower than deciding whether the tests adequately assess the software.

terms.deep_definition: An accurate report of a poorly tested change can pass a report-faithfulness audit. Assessing the underlying change requires additional evidence and appropriate checks.
terms.scope_note: An audit establishes the agreement between a report and a record.
terms.example: The closeout faithfulness audit compares a session's report against its trace.

terms.label: authority
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: Authority is the recognised basis for settling a particular question or permitting an action.
terms.reader_preview: Authority is the recognised basis for settling a particular question or permitting an action.
terms.card_definition: Plectis assigns authority by subject. Source code establishes what an implementation contains; an execution record reports a captured run; the operator's instructions determine intended scope. Each source can settle some questions and leave others unanswered.
terms.reader_rule: Identify both the source and the kind of decision it can support.
terms.deep_definition: A generated page can help you find authoritative material, but a convenient or confident summary does not acquire the authority of the source it describes.
terms.scope_note: Authority covers the decision class, artifact, time, and conditions named by its governing contract.
terms.example: The term registry is authoritative for glossary membership, while the generated glossary page is not.
terms.non_example: Confidence, prominence, or repetition does not create authority.

terms.label: axiom
terms.meaning_boundary: An ai_workflow axiom is a promoted system constraint. It is not automatically a mathematical axiom, self-evident truth, or externally accepted principle.
terms.short_definition: An axiom is a starting assumption of a mathematical theory; Plectis also uses the word for a fundamental system rule.
terms.reader_preview: An axiom is a starting assumption of a mathematical theory; Plectis also uses the word for a fundamental system rule.
terms.card_definition: A mathematical proof derives its conclusion from its hypotheses and underlying axioms. On the software pages, a system axiom instead states a design constraint that other rules are expected to preserve.
terms.reader_rule: The surrounding subject determines which meaning is intended.
terms.deep_definition: For a Lean theorem, the relevant question is which logical assumptions its proof depends on. For a Plectis design rule, the question is how the implementation enforces it and what evidence shows that enforcement.
terms.scope_note: On maths pages, the mathematical or Lean sense. On doctrine pages, the system constraint sense. The same English word is kept so the collision stays visible.
terms.example: On the doctrine pages, AX-7 (typed partiality and refusal) is a system axiom. On a Lean page, Classical.choice is a mathematical axiom.

terms.reader_preview: A band is a named level of detail in a description, such as a brief label, a short summary, or a full explanation.

The vocabulary comes from the compression profiles and the navigation design that the public pages are generated from.

terms.label: barrier
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A mathematical barrier is an obstruction showing why a specified approach cannot establish its intended result under stated conditions.
terms.reader_preview: A mathematical barrier is an obstruction showing why a specified approach cannot establish its intended result under stated conditions.
terms.card_definition: A barrier theorem proves a limitation of a method or construction. In these papers, such results help identify which attempted routes have failed and what a future approach would have to change.
terms.reader_rule: Check the hypotheses and the precise class of approaches ruled out.
terms.deep_definition: A method failing does not show that the original problem is impossible. A barrier can be useful progress by preventing repetition and revealing which assumption caused the obstruction.
terms.scope_note: A barrier establishes that one route fails. It says nothing about routes it does not name.
terms.example: A proof that one proposed mechanism stays uniformly away from its target is a barrier to that mechanism; it does not rule out other mechanisms.
terms.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

terms.label: base
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A numeral base is the number whose powers determine place values; decimal uses ten and binary uses two.
terms.reader_preview: A numeral base is the number whose powers determine place values; decimal uses ten and binary uses two.
terms.card_definition: In an integer base b greater than one, the allowed digits are 0 through b−1. Places after the radix point have weights 1/b, 1/b², and so on. The papers also use b as the base in expressions such as bⁿ.
terms.reader_rule: Read the stated restrictions on b before applying an argument about digits or divisibility.
terms.deep_definition: Changing the base changes an expansion's digits and repetition pattern while leaving the represented number itself unchanged.
terms.scope_note: Base covers the explicitly named numeral or exponential base in one series, expansion, or theorem.
terms.example: In base two, 0.11 represents 1/2 + 1/4; at a rational base such as 3/2, power-based series need the separate assumptions stated in the paper.
terms.non_example: Base here does not mean a database, code superclass, or physical support.

terms.label: basis
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage in linear algebra (a generating set of a vector space). It is not the named inputs a claim is derived from; that sense is named_basis.
terms.short_definition: In linear algebra, a basis is a set of vectors from which every vector in a space has a unique finite linear combination.
terms.reader_preview: In linear algebra, a basis is a set of vectors from which every vector in a space has a unique finite linear combination.
terms.card_definition: The two requirements are spanning and linear independence: the vectors reach the whole space, and none can be expressed using the others. For the ordinary plane, one horizontal and one vertical unit vector form a basis.
terms.reader_rule: Other fields use “basis” for different structures, so the surrounding definition matters.
terms.deep_definition: Plectis also speaks of a named basis for a claim: the stated sources or assumptions supporting it. That use does not assert a linear-algebra structure.
terms.scope_note: Linear-algebra sense: a basis of a vector space, not a numeral base.
terms.example: The vectors (1,0) and (0,1) form a basis of the plane.
terms.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

terms.label: binary expansion
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A binary expansion writes a number with digits 0 and 1, using powers of two as place values.
terms.reader_preview: A binary expansion writes a number with digits 0 and 1, using powers of two as place values.
terms.card_definition: For example, 0.101 in binary is 1/2 + 0/4 + 1/8, or 5/8. The digit positions turn questions about a real number into questions about a sequence of zeros and ones.
terms.reader_rule: In base two, rational numbers have eventually repeating expansions.
terms.deep_definition: Numbers with a terminating expansion also have an alternative ending in repeating ones. Arguments about uniqueness or periodicity must account for this familiar ambiguity.
terms.scope_note: A binary expansion covers one number under the standard base-two representation convention.
terms.example: The binary totient series is studied through constraints that rationality would impose on its eventual binary digits.
terms.non_example: A decimal approximation printed with zeros and ones is not automatically a binary expansion.

terms.label: bound
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A bound is a value that a quantity is proved to stay above or below under stated conditions.
terms.reader_preview: A bound is a value that a quantity is proved to stay above or below under stated conditions.
terms.card_definition: An upper bound M gives x ≤ M; a lower bound m gives m ≤ x. Bounds can also depend on a parameter, such as the number of terms in a sum.
terms.reader_rule: A bound need not equal the quantity it controls or be the best possible bound.
terms.deep_definition: In these papers, bounds often control the error left after a finite calculation, allowing a statement about an infinite process to follow from finite information.
terms.scope_note: A bound covers the quantity and range it is proved for.
terms.example: If a nonnegative tail is at most 1/100, then the partial sum approximates the full sum with error no larger than 1/100.
terms.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

terms.label: bridge
terms.meaning_boundary: Bridge means the repository's bounded external-worker transport. It is not a physical bridge, a generic software bridge, or an autonomous controller.
terms.short_definition: A bridge is Plectis's mechanism for sending a bounded task to an outside worker and returning its response.
terms.reader_preview: A bridge is Plectis's mechanism for sending a bounded task to an outside worker and returning its response.
terms.card_definition: The controlling agent selects the instructions and context to send. The returned material is then assessed before it is incorporated into the working system. This exchange can support an external reasoning or research pass.
terms.reader_rule: The bridge itself does not grant the outside worker direct control of the local files.
terms.deep_definition: The worker's answer remains a proposal or source of evidence until the receiving agent checks it and performs any authorised changes.
terms.scope_note: The term covers the external worker lane and its dispatch and response machinery. A reader meets it wherever the site describes work sent to separate workers, such as parallel reasoning, research runs, or bulk population, and in the runtime component that carries this work across phases.
terms.example: The Bridge Phase Continuity Runtime is one concrete instance: the runtime unit that carries bounded bridge work across phases of a task and keeps a single dispatch-and-response round coherent over time.

example_route.label: Bridge Phase Continuity Runtime
example_route.gloss: open the runtime component that carries bridge work across phases

terms.non_example: A bridge is not the system's conductor and not an autonomous agent that explores the codebase, runs many steps, or makes changes by itself. It is a one-packet-out, one-packet-back transport with all orchestration held outside it.

terms.label: bundle
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A bundle is a group of related files packaged together for inspection or use.
terms.reader_preview: A bundle is a group of related files packaged together for inspection or use.
terms.card_definition: For a Plectis component, an evidence bundle can include the source code, test inputs, and result record associated with a run. Keeping them together lets a reader inspect which inputs were used, which checks ran, and what those checks returned.
terms.reader_rule: The bundle's inventory and source versions determine what it actually contains.
terms.deep_definition: A bundle may document a recorded run or provide material for repeating it. The accompanying instructions should say which of those uses it supports.
terms.scope_note: A bundle describes the files and checks it contains; its evidence supports only the behaviour those checks cover.
terms.example: A component's exported bundle carries its source bodies under source_modules/, the fixtures it read, and the result record from the run, each digest-checked against live source.
terms.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

terms.label: canonicalisation
terms.meaning_boundary: The staged meaning used here is Terence Tao's, from Mathematics in the age of AI (arXiv:2608.16753). This site does not own or redefine that stage; community acceptance remains external.
terms.short_definition: Canonicalisation is the process of putting something into a standard, representative form.
terms.reader_preview: Canonicalisation is the process of putting something into a standard, representative form.
terms.card_definition: In the mathematical research discussion here, it means consolidating a result into a natural statement and an understood proof that others can reuse. Equivalent formulations and routine supporting lemmas may become part of one clearer account.
terms.reader_rule: A repository can simplify its own presentation, but it cannot declare that the mathematical community has adopted it.
terms.deep_definition: This is a later question than whether a proof checks: it concerns which formulation and explanation become useful, recognised tools for other work.
terms.scope_note: The word is Tao's. The local use is: do not pretend a first checked proof is the community's finished form of the result.
terms.example: A later paper that rebuilds a first formal proof around the natural statement and the shortest argument would be an attempt to assist canonicalisation; whether the community adopts that form is external.
terms.non_example: Kernel acceptance of the first proof script is verification, not canonicalisation.

terms.label: care
terms.meaning_boundary: Care is an operational judgment trait in the Type A register. The term does not claim emotion, consciousness, human virtue, or an external psychological classification.
terms.short_definition: Care means attending to the people, correctness, and future maintenance affected by a piece of work.
terms.reader_preview: Care means attending to the people, correctness, and future maintenance affected by a piece of work.
terms.card_definition: Plectis uses the word as a practical standard for an agent's conduct. A change should be understandable, checked to the appropriate extent, and left in a state that another person can continue.
terms.reader_rule: Care is expressed through decisions and follow-through, rather than through enthusiastic language.
terms.deep_definition: For example, preserving unrelated edits and updating an instruction made inaccurate by a change both reduce avoidable costs for the next person working on the system.
terms.scope_note: Care covers the maintenance-and-continuity dimension of how agents act on the system: protecting the next person or agent from re-deriving lost context, inheriting stale facts, or losing the original intent. A reader meets it across the agent reliability and continuity material, and in the audits that check whether a completed task left an honest, faithful record.
terms.example: The Agent Completion Faithfulness Audit is care made concrete: it checks that a finished task left an accurate record of what was actually done, rather than a tidy claim the underlying files do not support.

example_route.label: Agent Completion Faithfulness Audit
example_route.gloss: open the audit that checks a finished task left an honest record

terms.non_example: Care is not sentiment, politeness, or a general value statement about doing good work. It is a specific obligation to leave upkeep behind: provenance, validation, and closeout records that the next agent can rely on.

relationships.gloss: Care is one trait supporting live controller judgment.
Care becomes practical through situated judgment and cheap truthful surfaces.
Care-driven local lessons should move to the owning plane when reusable.

source_refs.gloss: Codex-facing closeout and common-sense contract.
Claude-facing continuity and care posture.
Entry-surface compression rule that keeps care routeable rather than adapter-bloated.

terms.label: catalog
terms.meaning_boundary: On the architecture page, catalog is the spine step after project: the governed collection of patterns the system can bind. It is not a bibliography and not the skill catalog.
terms.short_definition: A catalog is an organised inventory; on Plectis's architecture page it lists patterns available for use in the system.
terms.reader_preview: A catalog is an organised inventory; on Plectis's architecture page it lists patterns available for use in the system.
terms.card_definition: Each catalog entry identifies a pattern and provides the information needed to select it. The architecture then connects the selected pattern to requirements, an implementation route, and evidence from its use.
terms.reader_rule: This particular catalog is distinct from the site's collection of papers or skills.
terms.deep_definition: Generating the inventory from registered source material makes omissions and stale entries easier to detect, although the generated catalog still needs to be refreshed and checked.
terms.scope_note: Spine catalog and the public pattern-catalog contract.

terms.label: certificate
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A certificate is data that a specified checker can use to verify a particular claim.
terms.reader_preview: A certificate is data that a specified checker can use to verify a particular claim.
terms.card_definition: The data might provide a witness, a calculation trace, or the finite cases needed for a result. Producing the certificate and checking it can be separate tasks, with different costs and trust requirements.
terms.reader_rule: The guarantee depends on what the checker verifies and how that check connects to the claim.
terms.deep_definition: A collection of verified cases establishes a general theorem only when a further argument shows that those cases cover everything the theorem asserts.
terms.scope_note: A certificate covers the finite case it encodes.
terms.example: The corpus carries generated certificates for the finite cases, each checked by the Lean kernel.
terms.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

terms.label: Challenge/Solution pair
terms.meaning_boundary: On the landing and coding-agents page, each Comparator or Palomar entry is a self-contained Challenge/Solution pair. It is not a generic contest prompt.
terms.short_definition: A Challenge/Solution pair packages a precise Lean problem with a proposed solution that can be checked against it.
terms.reader_preview: A Challenge/Solution pair packages a precise Lean problem with a proposed solution that can be checked against it.
terms.card_definition: The challenge states the required result and allowed assumptions. The solution supplies the implementation or proof intended to meet that requirement. Plectis uses the pair as an independently inspectable unit in its Comparator and Palomar material.
terms.reader_rule: The solution must satisfy the actual challenge, including its hypotheses and restrictions.
terms.deep_definition: Checking one pair establishes that result within its stated setting. It does not automatically settle neighbouring statements or the original open problem from which the challenge was derived.
terms.scope_note: Lean Comparator and Palomar release entries.

terms.label: check
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A check is an examination of whether something satisfies a stated condition.
terms.reader_preview: A check is an examination of whether something satisfies a stated condition.
terms.card_definition: On this site, a check usually has a runnable command, specified inputs, and a recorded result. It may test a behaviour, validate a file, compare copies, or verify a proof.
terms.reader_rule: The result should say what was examined and which condition passed or failed.
terms.deep_definition: Useful checks can distinguish relevant failures from success. Reading a recorded result tells you about that run; repeating the command supplies evidence about your own copy and environment.
terms.scope_note: A check establishes its own outcome on its own inputs, and nothing wider.
terms.example: Each of the public components ships one check, its command written out in full.
terms.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

terms.label: checker
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A checker is a program or procedure that evaluates an input against specified rules.
terms.reader_preview: A checker is a program or procedure that evaluates an input against specified rules.
terms.card_definition: A syntax checker, link checker, and proof checker each answer a different question. Their outputs are useful when the rules, inputs, and failure conditions are clear enough to inspect.
terms.reader_rule: A pass establishes satisfaction of the implemented rules, subject to the checker's own correctness.
terms.deep_definition: The rules may still omit something important to the wider task. Plectis therefore connects checker results to specific claims rather than treating every pass as general approval.
terms.scope_note: The term covers automated and procedural validation tools shown in the site's evidence chain.
terms.example: The internal-link checker rejects a page whose href points to no generated target.
terms.non_example: A human opinion without a stated evaluation rule is not an automated checker result.

terms.label: Chinese remainder theorem
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: The Chinese remainder theorem solves simultaneous congruences with pairwise coprime positive moduli.
terms.reader_preview: The Chinese remainder theorem solves simultaneous congruences with pairwise coprime positive moduli.
terms.card_definition: It says that any prescribed remainders occur together in exactly one class modulo the product of the moduli. For example, x ≡ 1 modulo 2 and x ≡ 2 modulo 3 combine to x ≡ 5 modulo 6.
terms.reader_rule: Without coprimality, the prescribed remainders must satisfy compatibility conditions.
terms.deep_definition: The papers use the theorem to arrange several divisibility conditions at once. It gives a controlled arithmetic construction rather than merely evidence that a computer found one suitable integer.
terms.scope_note: Without coprimality, the prescribed remainders must satisfy compatibility conditions.
terms.example: Representative source: sites/microcosm/maths/problems/erdos_243.html::line 116.
terms.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

terms.label: circuit-break
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: To circuit-break a process is to interrupt a loop that would otherwise keep running or reinforcing itself.
terms.reader_preview: To circuit-break a process is to interrupt a loop that would otherwise keep running or reinforcing itself.
terms.card_definition: In Plectis's research discussion, the loop is self-confirmation: the same people or tools produce work and judge its value. An outside reader can interrupt that loop by questioning the evidence, interpretation, or direction.
terms.reader_rule: An interruption prompts reassessment; it does not itself decide which conclusion is true.
terms.deep_definition: Automated checks remain useful for errors they can detect. Independent judgement addresses questions of meaning and value that repeating the internal checks may never raise.
terms.scope_note: Names the interruption of a self-feeding process. It does not name the content of the resulting judgement.
terms.example: A mathematician reading one problem page and saying the main lemma is a known result would circuit-break the author's self-assessment.
terms.non_example: Prompting a model to praise the repository is not a circuit-break; it continues the same loop.

terms.label: claim
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A claim is an assertion that can be examined for truth or support.
terms.reader_preview: A claim is an assertion that can be examined for truth or support.
terms.card_definition: Plectis records what a component or mathematical result is said to establish and links that wording to evidence. This makes it possible to compare the public explanation with the source, proof, or recorded test.
terms.reader_rule: The strength of the wording should match the strength and scope of the evidence.
terms.deep_definition: For example, a successful test on specified inputs supports that tested behaviour. A claim covering every possible input requires a different argument or a suitable proof.
terms.scope_note: A claim establishes nothing by itself. Its evidence does, and only as far as the evidence reaches.
terms.example: A component states one claim and includes one check; the release gate refuses wording that reaches past what the check ran.
terms.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

terms.label: claim registry
terms.meaning_boundary: Here, the claim registry is the reviewed map from public mathematical claims to their status, formal support, and open boundary; it is not an inventory of every Lean declaration.
terms.short_definition: A claim registry is a structured list of assertions and the evidence, scope, and status attached to each.
terms.reader_preview: A claim registry is a structured list of assertions and the evidence, scope, and status attached to each.
terms.card_definition: For the formal mathematics, it connects reader-facing statements to particular declarations or other supporting material. This gives reviewers a way to check that the explanation says what the mathematics actually establishes.
terms.reader_rule: Registration records how a claim is presented and supported; it is not peer review.
terms.deep_definition: When the wording or proof changes, their connection must be checked again. A large number of formal declarations does not by itself imply an equally large number of distinct research contributions.
terms.scope_note: The registry covers the claims recorded in it, not everything the corpus contains.
terms.example: The registry records each public mathematical claim with its status, formal support, and remaining open boundary, while keeping statements explicitly marked as not claimed separate.
terms.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

terms.label: clearing denominators
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: Clearing denominators multiplies an equation or expression by a suitable nonzero common denominator to remove its fractions.
terms.reader_preview: Clearing denominators multiplies an equation or expression by a suitable nonzero common denominator to remove its fractions.
terms.card_definition: For example, multiplying x/2 + y/3 = 1 by 6 gives 3x + 2y = 6. Every term must receive the same multiplier for the equation to remain equivalent.
terms.reader_rule: If a denominator contains a variable, its nonzero condition must be preserved.
terms.deep_definition: The papers use this operation to obtain integer equations from rational quantities. Divisibility and congruence arguments can then study the resulting integers without losing the original denominator assumptions.
terms.scope_note: If a denominator contains a variable, its nonzero condition must be preserved.

terms.short_definition: To clone a repository is to create a local copy of its files and Git history, with options to limit what is downloaded.
terms.reader_preview: To clone a repository is to create a local copy of its files and Git history, with options to limit what is downloaded.

terms.label: closed route
terms.meaning_boundary: A closed route is a fact about one method. It says nothing about whether the problem is true or false.
terms.short_definition: A closed route is a recorded approach that has been ruled out within a stated set of assumptions or methods.
terms.reader_preview: A closed route is a recorded approach that has been ruled out within a stated set of assumptions or methods.
terms.card_definition: The working records keep the reason for closure, such as a counterexample or a proved obstruction. This lets later researchers understand the failure before trying a similar idea.
terms.reader_rule: Closure applies to the described approach, not automatically to the original problem.
terms.deep_definition: A materially different method or hypothesis may avoid the obstruction. The record should make clear what would have to change, and whether the closure rests on proof, exact calculation, or weaker evidence.
terms.scope_note: Covers failed approaches recorded in the papers and working records.
terms.example: For #249, the positive rank-one Möbius–Mersenne mechanism is a closed route: its cone sits a uniform gap above the target value.
terms.non_example: An approach abandoned for lack of time is not a closed route, because nothing was shown.

terms.label: closeout

terms.label: cofinal
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A subset of an ordered set is cofinal if it reaches at least as far as every element of that set.
terms.reader_preview: A subset of an ordered set is cofinal if it reaches at least as far as every element of that set.
terms.card_definition: More precisely, for each x there is an element y in the subset with x ≤ y. For indices in the natural numbers, this means that qualifying indices occur arbitrarily far out.
terms.reader_rule: Cofinality does not mean that every sufficiently large index qualifies.
terms.deep_definition: For example, the even natural numbers are cofinal among all natural numbers. This distinction matters when a proof needs infinitely many suitable indices rather than a property that eventually holds everywhere.
terms.scope_note: Cofinal is about indices going to infinity, not about density or frequency.
terms.example: The even numbers occur cofinally among the whole numbers.

terms.reader_rule: “Cold” describes missing context, not a lack of reasoning ability.

terms.label: combinatorics

terms.short_definition: Combinatorics studies how discrete objects can be selected, arranged, counted, and related.

terms.card_definition: Typical questions concern subsets, permutations, graphs, and patterns that must occur in sufficiently large collections. Some problems ask for an exact count; others ask whether a configuration exists at all.

terms.label: conditional reduction
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A conditional reduction proves that a target statement follows if a specified further condition holds.
terms.reader_preview: A conditional reduction proves that a target statement follows if a specified further condition holds.
terms.card_definition: The implication can be a complete theorem even while the condition remains unresolved. The reduction is useful when it exposes a more tractable question or clarifies exactly what additional evidence is needed.
terms.reader_rule: The target is still open until the required condition is established or another proof is found.
terms.deep_definition: A one-way implication need not give an equivalent problem. The new condition may be stronger than the target, so its difficulty and plausibility need separate assessment.
terms.scope_note: A conditional reduction establishes an implication, not its conclusion.
terms.example: A proof that the target follows from a still-open summability estimate is a conditional reduction: the implication is established, while the target remains open until the estimate is proved.

terms.label: conditional theorem
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A conditional theorem proves a conclusion under stated hypotheses.
terms.reader_preview: A conditional theorem proves a conclusion under stated hypotheses.
terms.card_definition: Mathematical theorems commonly have hypotheses. Here the label is especially useful when an important hypothesis remains unproved, so the theorem establishes an implication without yet establishing the desired conclusion on its own.

terms.label: digestion
terms.meaning_boundary: The staged meaning of digestion used here is Terence Tao's, from Mathematics in the age of AI (arXiv:2608.16753). This site does not own or redefine that stage; it only says how it tries to help authors assist it. Community digestion and acceptance remain external.
terms.short_definition: Mathematical digestion is the process of understanding a result well enough to place it in the field and use it in further work.
terms.reader_preview: Mathematical digestion is the process of understanding a result well enough to place it in the field and use it in further work.
terms.card_definition: It includes identifying the main idea, checking how the hypotheses matter, connecting the result to earlier work, and finding useful applications or reformulations. The site's discussion follows the distinction between verifying a proof and making its mathematics usable.
terms.reader_rule: A checked proof and a published paper can support this process without completing it.
terms.deep_definition: Clear explanations, failed approaches, and precise open questions help other mathematicians assess and continue the work. Community uptake cannot be awarded by a repository's own checks.
terms.scope_note: The word is Tao's. The local use is: keep the record that would help a mathematician digest the work. The local use is not: declare the work digested.
terms.example: A reader who can explain the main argument, identify its limitations, and apply the result to a new question has understood more than whether a formal proof passes its checker.
terms.non_example: A long formally verified proof with no account of the hard step, the false starts, or what remains open is not digestion, however correct it is.

terms.label: discrete mathematics
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: Discrete mathematics studies objects with separate elements, such as integers, graphs, and finite arrangements.
terms.reader_preview: Discrete mathematics studies objects with separate elements, such as integers, graphs, and finite arrangements.
terms.card_definition: Its questions include counting configurations, finding paths in networks, and proving properties of integer sequences. The objects may be finite or infinite; “discrete” does not mean “finite”.
terms.reader_rule: The relevant structure is determined by the definitions of the problem.
terms.deep_definition: Number theory and combinatorics supply many of the discrete methods used in these papers. Arguments may still involve continuous tools, such as real limits or analytic estimates, to study discrete objects.
terms.scope_note: Discrete mathematics covers the discrete objects and relations named by the problem or theory.
terms.example: Integers and finite graphs are standard objects of discrete mathematics.
terms.non_example: A problem about a continuously varying physical field is not discrete merely because a computer samples it.

terms.label: divergence
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: A sequence or series diverges when it does not converge in the sense being considered.
terms.reader_preview: A sequence or series diverges when it does not converge in the sense being considered.
terms.card_definition: For real sequences, failure to approach a finite limit can mean growing without bound or oscillating indefinitely. A series diverges when its sequence of partial sums fails to converge.
terms.reader_rule: Individual terms tending to zero do not ensure that their sum converges.
terms.deep_definition: The harmonic series is a standard example: its terms shrink to zero while its partial sums grow without bound. Papers should specify whether “diverges” means unbounded growth or another failure of convergence.
terms.scope_note: Divergence covers the exact sequence, series, parameter, and convergence notion named by the statement.
terms.example: If partial sums grow without bound, the series diverges in the ordinary sense.
terms.non_example: A slowly converging sequence is not divergent merely because a finite computation has not reached its limit.

terms.label: divisibility
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: Divisibility is the relation in which one integer is an exact integer multiple of another.
terms.reader_preview: Divisibility is the relation in which one integer is an exact integer multiple of another.
terms.card_definition: The notation a ∣ b means that b = ak for some integer k. For example, 3 divides 12 because 12 = 3·4, while 5 does not divide 12.
terms.reader_rule: The direction matters: a ∣ b does not generally imply b ∣ a.
terms.deep_definition: With this algebraic definition, every integer divides zero and zero divides only zero. The papers often impose positivity to exclude such cases, then use divisibility to track denominator cancellation, congruences, and prime factors.
terms.scope_note: The direction matters: a ∣ b does not generally imply b ∣ a.

terms.label: divisor
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: An integer d divides an integer n if n = d·k for some integer k.
terms.reader_preview: An integer d divides an integer n if n = d·k for some integer k.
terms.card_definition: For example, 3 divides 12 because 12 = 3·4. Number-theory statements usually specify positive divisors, while the divisibility relation itself can also involve negative integers or zero.
terms.reader_rule: The notation d ∣ n means “d divides n”.
terms.deep_definition: A divisor is an exact factor, so there is no remainder. With the stated algebraic definition, every integer divides zero, and zero divides only zero; additional positivity hypotheses often exclude these edge cases.
terms.scope_note: Divisor covers the integer relation and conventions stated in the surrounding theorem or definition.
terms.example: 3 is a divisor of 12 because 12 = 3 × 4.
terms.non_example: 5 is not a divisor of 12 because no integer multiplied by 5 equals 12.

terms.reader_preview: The epistemic control plane is a proposed system layer that uses evidence and uncertainty to govern which actions may proceed.

terms.label: equality
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: An equality states that two expressions represent the same value or mathematical object.
terms.reader_preview: An equality states that two expressions represent the same value or mathematical object.
terms.card_definition: For example, 1/2 = 2/4 compares different expressions for the same number. Equality depends on the setting: two functions are equal when they agree as functions, not merely at a few tested inputs.
terms.reader_rule: Distinguish equality from an approximation or a one-way implication.
terms.deep_definition: In Lean, equality is itself a proposition that can require a proof. Two expressions that simplify to the same form may be equal for a more direct reason than expressions requiring a substantial theorem.
terms.scope_note: An equality covers the two expressions, domain, and assumptions stated around it.
terms.example: The equality 12 = 3 × 4 witnesses that 3 divides 12.
terms.non_example: Two decimal approximations that look alike are not necessarily exactly equal.

terms.label: equation
terms.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
terms.short_definition: An equation is a mathematical statement that two expressions are equal.
terms.reader_preview: An equation is a mathematical statement that two expressions are equal.
terms.card_definition: It can specify a relation, define a quantity, or ask which values make the equality true. For example, x² = 4 has solutions x = 2 and x = −2 over the real numbers.
terms.reader_rule: The permitted domain and assumptions determine what counts as a solution.
terms.deep_definition: Some equations are identities that hold for every allowed value; others hold only for particular values. A displayed equality in a proof may express a justified transformation rather than a problem to solve.
terms.scope_note: An equation covers the expressions, unknowns, domain, and constraints stated in its formulation.
terms.example: In a denominator argument, an equation obtained by assuming a series rational converts an infinite sum into an exact relation among integers.
terms.non_example: An inequality such as x < 3 compares ordered values; it does not assert equality and is not an equation.

terms.label: equivalence
terms.meaning_boundary: Equivalence means that each of the two named statements implies the other under the same stated domain and hypotheses. It does not follow from similarity, shared examples, or a one-way implication.
terms.short_definition: Two statements are logically equivalent when each implies the other under the same assumptions.
terms.reader_preview: Two statements are logically equivalent when each implies the other under the same assumptions.
terms.card_definition: To establish P ↔ Q, one proves both P → Q and Q → P. Either statement can then replace the other within that setting, although one may be easier to understand or use.
terms.reader_rule: A single implication gives a reduction in one direction, not an equivalence.
terms.deep_definition: The papers use equivalences to compare reformulations of open problems. An equivalent reformulation preserves the unresolved question; proving the equivalence alone does not establish either side unconditionally.
terms.scope_note: An equivalence covers the two named statements under their common hypotheses and domain.
terms.example: An irrationality question may be equivalent to the impossibility of an eventually periodic digit pattern.
terms.non_example: Similarity, shared examples, or a one-way implication does not establish equivalence.

terms.label: Paul Erdős

terms.short_definition: Paul Erdős was a mathematician known for work in number theory, combinatorics, probability, and related fields.

terms.label: Euler's theorem (modular arithmetic)
